sources.title: Independent recursive enumeration and boundary validation

claims.text: The source asks for a total coin-change combination count but does not preserve unlimited-use, input-validation or numeric-width constraints; the candidate marks these as its executable contract.

Coin-outer iteration avoids counting denomination order as separate arrangements, while ascending amount permits repeated use of the current denomination; exact execution matches independent enumeration and is invariant to denomination input order.
The empty-combination seed, empty denomination boundaries, invalid denominations and exact large-count behavior are covered by deterministic executable validation under the declared contract.

validation.command: compile exact candidate Java block and compare with independent recursive enumeration and boundary assertions
validation.reported_stdout: PASS independent recursive=2400 permutations=7200 zero-empty=1 positive-empty=0 invalid-denominations=rejected
checks: 2400 deterministic small cases match independent recursive enumeration
zero amount with no coins returns one empty combination
positive amount with no coins returns zero
duplicate and zero denominations are rejected by the declared contract

boundary_tests.expected: same unordered-combination count for all permutations

findings: The preserved source asks only for total combination count for an amount and coin denominations; unlimited reuse, denomination uniqueness, invalid-input policy and numeric bounds are not preserved source facts.
The candidate labels those missing conditions as an explicit executable contract.
Coin-outer iteration prevents denomination order from creating duplicate arrangements, while ascending amount permits unlimited reuse of the current denomination.
The dp[0]=1 empty-combination seed and complete-knapsack versus 0/1 traversal boundary are explained.
Independent execution matches recursive enumeration on 2400 deterministic cases and 7200 input-order permutations, including explicit zero/empty and invalid-denomination boundaries.
BigInteger avoids an unsupported fixed-width result bound.
